title: Potato vs Sweet Potato: Nutrition Differences

seo.title: Potato vs Sweet Potato: Calories, Fiber and Nutrients
seo.meta_description: Potatoes and sweet potatoes have very similar calories and carbs. Orange sweet potato stands out for beta-carotene; potato often provides more potassium.
seo.search_intent: Compare cooked potato and sweet potato without exaggerating small calorie and carbohydrate differences.

excerpt: Potatoes and sweet potatoes are much closer in calories and carbohydrate than their reputations suggest: both are around 90 calories and 20–21 grams of carbohydrate per 100 grams cooked. The interesting difference is micronutrients: orange sweet potato stands out for beta-carotene, while potato often provides more potassium and vitamin C.
content_html:
Sweet potatoes have earned a reputation as the “healthier” version of white potatoes, but if the comparison starts with calories and carbohydrate, the surprise is how little separates them. Both are starchy tubers and, cooked with little added fat, land in almost the same range.

The meaningful difference is not calories; it is micronutrients. Orange sweet potato stands out for beta-carotene, while potato often provides more potassium and vitamin C.

Per 100 grams cooked, they are almost tied

PotatoOrange sweet potato
Calories~90–95~90
Carbohydrate~21 g~21 g
Protein~2–2.5 g~2 g
Fiber~2 g~3 g

For energy and carbohydrate, the result is essentially a draw. Sweet potato may provide about 1 extra gram of fiber per 100 grams; potato has a few tenths more protein. Neither small difference changes a meal by itself.

The orange color tells a genuinely different story

Orange flesh signals a high concentration of carotenoids, especially beta-carotene, which the body can convert to vitamin A. A normal serving of orange sweet potato can provide several times the daily reference amount of provitamin A.

That is not true to the same degree for every variety. White and purple sweet potatoes have different pigment profiles, so “sweet potato” is not one identical nutrient composition either.

Potato often wins on potassium

A cooked potato with skin can exceed 500 mg of potassium per 100 grams, while many sweet potatoes are closer to 300–400 mg. Across a 7-ounce serving, the difference can exceed 200 mg.

Cooking matters here too: boiling and discarding the water can remove some potassium from either tuber.

Vitamin C often favors potato as well

Potatoes contribute a meaningful amount of vitamin C, although storage and long cooking can reduce it. Sweet potatoes contain vitamin C too, but often less in comparable varieties and preparations.

Sweet taste does not mean dramatically more carbohydrate

During cooking, enzymes and heat can convert some sweet-potato starch into sugars, which makes it taste sweeter. Total carbohydrate still remains around 21 grams per 100 grams—almost identical to potato.

Flavor can change substantially without calories changing in the same proportion.

Cooking method matters more than which tuber you choose

A potato and a sweet potato baked with little oil are both around 90 calories per 100 grams. Frying removes water and adds oil, so French fries or sweet-potato chips can easily exceed 300 calories per 100 grams.

That increase of more than 200 calories is far larger than the difference between the two tubers when simply cooked.

What to remember

Potatoes and sweet potatoes are practically tied in calories and carbs. Orange sweet potato stands out for beta-carotene and somewhat more fiber; potato often provides more potassium and vitamin C. Alternating them makes more sense than turning one into the “good” version and the other into the “bad” one.

faq.question: Which has more calories, potato or sweet potato?
faq.answer: Cooked with little added fat, they are essentially tied at around 90 calories per 100 grams.

faq.question: Does sweet potato have more sugar?
faq.answer: It tastes sweeter because some starch is converted to sugars during cooking, but total carbohydrate is very similar to potato.

faq.question: Which has more vitamin A?
faq.answer: Orange-fleshed sweet potato by a very large margin because it is rich in beta-carotene.
